passage: From our balcony I saw the Class 4 boys near the gate and heard Charu yelling at another boy, his face red and his fists at his sides. “Give it back! Give it back!” The other boy just held a small green eraser high. I could not tell whether Charu was furious or scared, or simply wanted someone to listen. He didn't hit anyone. After a bit he stopped, turned and walked quickly to the guard's booth, still breathing hard, and said something to the guard, who walked back with him. The eraser was handed over. Charu's voice was shaking. I'm Rekha, his neighbour.

qa.q: What did the other boy hold up?
qa.a: A small green eraser.

qa.q: What might Charu have been feeling while he shouted, according to Rekha?
qa.a: Rekha could not be sure if he was furious, scared or just wanting to be heard, since his voice was loud and shaking but he did not hit anyone.

qa.q: What did Charu do that was safer than shouting back or fighting?
qa.a: He stepped away and went to the guard for help, which got the eraser returned without a fight.

qa.q: How might the other boy have seen Charu's shouting?
qa.a: He may have been startled, since a raised voice can feel threatening even when the shouter is scared or wants to be heard.

grounding: A child recognises shouting as anger, fear or a wish to be heard and responds by stepping back and getting an adult.

passage:
Monday. Harsha's brother shouted at him in the corridor before the bell, so loudly that Gargi jumped. Harsha shouted back, and it got worse. Gargi watched from the stairs and did not know what to do.

Wednesday. Harsha shouted at Gargi about a lost notebook. She felt her heart thump, but she said, “I'll help look,” in a low voice and took a step back. Harsha stopped, panting. It turned out he had been afraid of Sir's anger.

Friday. Someone shouted a threat at Gargi's cousin near the bus. She did not shout back. She found Mrs. Gomes straight away and told her.

qa.q: On which day did Harsha shout at Gargi about a lost notebook?
qa.a: On Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Harsha probably feeling when he shouted about the notebook?
qa.a: He was afraid of Sir's anger, and the shouting covered that fear.

qa.q: What did Gargi learn to do across the three days?
qa.a: She stayed calm and stepped back when Harsha shouted, and when a real threat was shouted at her cousin she reported it to Mrs. Gomes at once.

qa.q: How might Gargi have felt when Harsha shouted at her about the notebook?
qa.a: She was frightened, since she felt her heart thump, but she stayed calm enough to offer help in a low voice.

grounding: Shouting can signal anger, fear or a wish to be heard, calm and stepping back are safer, and threats are reported.

passage: Yogesh, you shouted back at that boy today. Let your Binita Pishi tell you what I learned at your age. In our lane in Siliguri, a big boy called Montu started yelling at my little brother over a lost kite. His face was red, spit flying. Then he shouted, “Tomorrow I'll break your legs!” My brother froze. I wanted to scream back, and I was shaking. Instead I took my brother's hand, stepped back and walked straight home. I told our father everything, even the words about the legs. Baba went to Montu's house that same evening, and the next morning Montu came and said sorry to my brother.

qa.q: What was the argument about?
qa.a: The argument was about a lost kite.

qa.q: What was young Binita feeling when Montu shouted the threat?
qa.a: She felt frightened and angry, shaking and wanting to scream back.

qa.q: What choice did Binita make, and why was it safer?
qa.a: She stepped back with her brother, walked home and told their father everything, including the threat, so an adult could deal with it that evening.

qa.q: How might Binita's little brother have felt when she took his hand?
qa.a: He was probably still scared but relieved and safer with his sister leading him away.

grounding: Shows a child recognising angry shouting, stepping back instead of shouting back, and reporting a shouted threat to a parent.

passage: The power cut came just as Sumit and Chetan reached the fourth floor, and the stairwell went pitch dark. Sumit started yelling. “Why did you make us take the stairs? This is YOUR fault! Do something!” His voice cracked and bounced off the walls. Chetan's first instinct was to shout back. Then he heard Sumit's breathing: fast, ragged. He's not just angry. He's scared. Chetan kept his voice low. “Okay. Hold the railing. I've got my torch.” The little light came on. Sumit stopped yelling but was shaking. Chetan phoned the building guard, who came up with a big lamp and walked them both home.

qa.q: Which floor had the boys reached when the power cut came?
qa.a: They had reached the fourth floor.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling as he yelled in the dark?
qa.a: Sumit was frightened, as his fast, ragged breathing and cracking voice showed, even though it came out as anger.

qa.q: What did Chetan do that calmed things?
qa.a: He didn't shout back, spoke low, turned on his torch and phoned the building guard for help.

qa.q: What would change if Chetan had shouted back?
qa.a: Sumit's fear might have grown into a real fight in the dark stairwell, with no one getting help.

grounding: Shows a child recognising that a friend's shouting signals fear, staying calm instead of shouting back, and getting an adult.

passage: In the colony park in Pune, the cricket game fell apart when Abhinav threw down the bat and yelled, “NOBODY listens to me! I said the ball crossed the line!” He was red in the face, fists clenched. The others shouted back, and it got louder. Arohi stepped back from the crowd. She thought, He's angry, but he also just wants someone to hear him. She didn't shout. She walked to the bench where Mr Kulkarni, the building uncle who kept score, was sitting, and asked him to come. He listened to Abhinav first, then to the others. “Replay the ball,” he said. Abhinav picked up the bat, still sulking but quiet.

qa.q: Who kept score at the game?
qa.a: Mr Kulkarni, the building uncle, kept score.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling when he threw down the bat?
qa.a: Abhinav was angry and frustrated, and also desperate to be heard after being ignored.

qa.q: Why was Arohi's choice safer than shouting back?
qa.a: She stepped back and fetched a calm adult, who listened to both sides and settled the dispute.

qa.q: How did the other players react to Abhinav's yelling?
qa.a: They shouted back, which only made the argument louder.

grounding: Shows a child reading a friend's shouting as anger and a wish to be heard, stepping back and getting an adult instead of shouting back.

passage:
"GIVE IT BACK! That's MY bat!"
"Thomas, I only borrowed it for one over—"
"I said GIVE IT! Or I'll smash your face in!"
Jaya's heart thumped. She put the bat down on the grass and stepped back. "Okay. It's there. I'm getting Miss."
"Fine, go! Tell her!"

"Miss Kaur, Thomas shouted that he'd smash my face in."
Miss Kaur walked over at once. "Thomas. Threats are never okay. Tell me what's going on."
Thomas was gripping the bat, eyes wet. "It's my brother's. I promised him nobody else would touch it. If it cracks, he'll never lend me anything again."
"So you were scared. Next time, come to me first. And Jaya is owed an apology."

qa.q: Whose bat was it really?
qa.a: Thomas's brother's bat.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling behind his shouting?
qa.a: Angry, but mostly scared that the bat might crack and his brother would stop trusting him; his wet eyes show it.

qa.q: Why was Jaya's response safer than shouting back?
qa.a: She stayed calm, put the bat down, stepped back and fetched Miss Kaur, reporting the threat instead of answering it.

qa.q: How might Jaya feel after hearing why Thomas shouted?
qa.a: She may still feel shaken by the threat, but understanding his fear could make it easier to accept his apology.

grounding: It shows a child recognising that shouting can come from fear, stepping back and fetching a teacher, and reporting a shouted threat.
